articles.title: Is It Really Rude to Give Someone a Gift They Can’t Return?
articles.content:
The only gift my grandmother ever gave me was a pair of used underwear she picked up at a garage sale. I was 12. I’d love to tell you I’m exaggerating for comic effect, but that’s just the kind of lady she was: frugal, practical and oblivious to other people’s feelings.
Sadly, my gift-related trauma doesn’t stop there. There was also the $20 spa gift card someone gave me as a “special treat.” As far as I could tell, nothing on that spa’s menu cost $20 (unless you count the cucumber water, and I’m betting that was extra), and I was too broke to cover the difference. So the card lived in my wallet like a tiny, laminated taunt until the spa went out of business, at which point I cried real tears over the $20 I had essentially set on fire.
But the Incident, with a capital I, is the one that still makes my jaw clench. When my husband and I got married, we received a gift in a box that said it was an electric teakettle. We didn’t need a teakettle, so we did the responsible adult thing and returned it, and we were thrilled to walk out with $75 that we promptly spent on stuff we actually needed. Victory! Adulting! Then, a week later, the store called. The box had not contained a teakettle. It had contained a cut-glass Easter basket. Someone had regifted it to us, tucked inside a teakettle box like a Trojan horse of tackiness, and the cut-glass Easter basket, I was informed, was not returnable. So we had to go back and hand the store $75 for the privilege of owning a huge, hideous basket that we then had to figure out what to do with. I am still bitter. (Yes, I’ve already complained about this basket on this very site, and no, time has not healed anything.)
I tell you this so you understand that I come to the question of nonreturnable gifts with a certain amount of lived experience. Because here’s the thing: We are constantly told to be smart shoppers. Start early! Hunt for deals! Stock up in July! But a lot of the best deals come with a catch. It’s final sale … or clearance … or thrifted … or from a charming little shop in another state … or bought so far in advance that the return window slammed shut around Labor Day.
So is it actually rude to hand someone a gift they can’t swap? I have thoughts. Several. Mostly emotional. Let’s dig in to the actual etiquette of this, my feelings aside.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more etiquette, holidays, humor, cleaning, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.
Let’s start with the defense, because it’s stronger than you’d think.
First, a gift is a gift, not a lease. Somewhere along the way, we started treating the return option like a basic human right, right up there with running water and Wi-Fi. But for most of human history, people just handed each other stuff and the recipient said thank you. The exit ramp is a bonus, not a requirement.
Second, some of the best gifts are inherently nonreturnable. The hand-poured candle from the adorable shop in Vermont. The mug you found at a roadside stand. The sweater you grabbed at a price so low, you may have looked around for the hidden cameras. These gifts say “I saw this and thought of you” in a way that a shrink-wrapped, receipt-stapled whatever never will. Nobody has ever returned a souvenir. (And if they tried, the shop would be in Vermont.)
Third, and I want to be loud about this: Not everyone can afford to pay full price, and a gift giver should never be shamed for that. If the choice is between a clearance-rack scarf you can afford and nothing at all, the scarf is the generous, loving and perfectly polite option. Any etiquette rule that quietly requires you to spend more money isn’t an etiquette rule—it’s a tax. And the bottom line is that frugal is not a four-letter word.
Now for the prosecution, which is me, holding a cut-glass Easter basket.
A gift is supposed to make someone’s life a little better, not hand them a homework assignment. When you give something that can’t be returned, exchanged or swapped for the right size, you’ve placed a bet with their closet, their kitchen and their storage space, and they’re the ones who pay if you lose. They either keep it (hello, guilt!) or do the legwork of regifting, donating or reselling it, all while worrying you’ll find out. Meanwhile, you’re over here feeling virtuous about your $9 deal.
The sneakiest version of this is the giver who knows the gift is final sale and just crosses their fingers that nobody asks. That’s a game of Receipt Roulette, and the recipient never agreed to play.
It’s also worth remembering that for some people, the ability to return a gift has nothing to do with being picky. A returned gift can turn into groceries, a tank of gas or the thing they actually needed. A final-sale present may not look like a trap from the giver’s side, but it can feel exactly like one from the receiving end.
Welcome to the gray area. Population: all of us. These variables matter—here’s why.
So what about the deal-versus-safety-net question? If you’re torn between a pricier gift that can go back and a cheaper one that can’t, here’s my rule of thumb: For someone whose taste you know in your bones, grab the bargain. For someone whose taste is a mystery to you, pay for the safety net.
Do you announce “No returns!” when they unwrap it? No. Nobody wants a gift that comes with a legal disclaimer. “Enjoy! All sales final!” is not a sentiment you want written inside a card.
But if the recipient asks whether you have the receipt, you tell the truth, in one sentence, with a smile and an escape hatch: “It was final sale, so it’s yours forever, but if it’s not right, regift it, donate it or sell it. I will not be offended.” Asking for a gift receipt carries the same low-grade dread as getting a Venmo request for a $3 coffee, because suddenly everyone is doing math in front of a friend. Make it easy on them.
The truly rude move is the fib. “Oh, I must have lost it!” turns a bargain into a betrayal. And if you did get a gift receipt, tuck it in the box. That tiny slip of paper is the cheapest kindness in retail.
Thrifted gifts are having a moment, and the numbers suggest we’re a lot more open to receiving them than giving them. In a 2024 YouGov survey, three-quarters of 18- to 24-year-old U.K.-based respondents said they’d be happy to open a secondhand gift on Christmas morning, as would nearly half of people over 55. But when asked whether they’d actually buy a used present for someone else, most said no. A U.S. survey from the resale company thredUP (so take it with a grain of resale-flavored salt) found about two-thirds of Americans were open to receiving secondhand gifts as of 2021. So we’ll happily accept—we’re just squeamish about being the one who hands it over.
My take: Thrifted is fantastic when the secondhand-ness is the point. A vintage fondue pot that you hunted down for your fondue-obsessed friend? Thoughtful. A beautifully made wool coat in their exact size and color, which would cost $400 new? Genius. The rule is to clean it, package it with care, and for the love of all that is holy, make sure it’s not missing pieces or toting bedbug passengers. Used underwear remains, and I say this with experience, a hard no.
Is it really the thought that counts? Yes, but only if there was an actual thought, and not just “Oooh, $4.” I’ve ruled before that bringing store-bought food to a potluck isn’t rude, because showing up with some effort is what counts. Gifts work the same way. The price, the source and the packaging matter far less than whether you were paying attention to the person on the other end.
It is not rude to give someone a gift they can’t return. Clearance, thrifted, souvenir, final sale: all perfectly polite, and in many cases, the kindest thing a person on a budget can do. What is rude is the sneaking, the setting of traps and the getting weird about it afterward. So, in the spirit of the season, I give you three commandments:
1. Thou shalt not give a final-sale gift where size, shade or specs matter … unless you know them cold. Hand out the candles. Keep the leather boots on the returnable list.
2. Thou shalt tell the truth about the receipt. One sentence, no fibbing, plenty of grace.
3. Thou shalt not be offended by what happens next. Once it’s theirs, they can keep it, regift it or donate it. Gifts are freely given or they’re not gifts at all.
And if you absolutely must regift a cut-glass Easter basket, I beg you: Label the box honestly.

articles.title: Here’s the Real Reason Our Joints Crackle When We Wake Up in the Morning—And It’s Not (Always) About Age
articles.content:
One weird part of getting older is that at some point, it starts to take a little more effort to get going in the morning—and not just because we could probably use stand to hit the snooze button one more time. Our morning movements might become a little slower, a little more deliberate and even a little louder. Yep, that’s your ankles, knuckles, knees and necks crackling like a campfire.
Now, before you think I just called you ancient, some people just naturally have joints that crack as they move. My editor, for example, swears she was simply born that way and could never sneak up on her parents as a child, especially when walking down the stairs first thing in the morning.
So is this crackling OK, or is it a cause for concern? And why does it generally become more pronounced as we age? I spoke with Pamela Mehta, MD, a California-based orthopedic surgeon and sports medicine physician, to find out. Read on to learn the cause of those snaps, crackles and pops, as well as when they’re perfectly normal and when they could be a problem.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more health, humor, cleaning, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.
Very common! It even has a name: crepitus. (Which is a lot less awful than it sounds, I promise.) Crepitus can occur in virtually any body part with a joint, though it’s most common in the knees, shoulders, neck, ankles and knuckles, according to Dr. Mehta, who runs Resilience Orthopedics in San Jose, California. “You’ll hear it more in the first few movements you make in the morning because your joints feel stiffer after a night of not moving,” she explains. “Once you’re warmed up, this usually quiets down.”
Knee crepitus affects about 41% of the general population, but how often it occurs in other joints hasn’t been well established and isn’t as well researched. But we do know crepitus increases with age, since the lubricating cartilage between bony joints that keeps them moving smoothly (and quietly) wears away.
“It’s more common as we get older, because cartilage thins over time and your joints are stiffer and less elastic, so there is more for the joint to catch on,” Dr. Mehta says.
There are several possible reasons your joints sound like a bowl of Rice Krispies in the morning.
When we experience crepitus during our first movements of the morning, it’s usually because of gas in the synovial fluid. This fluid reduces friction between the bones in our joints.
“It’s often a tiny gas bubble releasing in the fluid that lubricates the joint,” Dr. Mehta says. “You can hear it, and you can sometimes feel it if you place your hand over the joint.”
When people have extra-flexible joints and a greater range of motion, they might experience more crepitus than others. “Muscle weakness or imbalances can also sometimes play a part,” Dr. Mehta says. “Many people find that the more they build balanced muscles around the joint, the less they notice it.”
As Dr. Mehta mentioned, the cracking in our joints tends to get more pronounced the older we get because our cartilage wears away and our joints get stiffer. “Arthritis is also more common as you age, and it can make the noise more noticeable,” Dr. Mehta says.
“A duller click or snap can be a tendon flicking over a bone, especially if it happens at the same point every time during a certain movement,” Dr. Mehta explains. Don’t worry—that kind of snap is usually normal and harmless. Tendons run close to bony points, and at a certain angle, a tendon can catch on the edge and then flick over it. The outside of the hip is common for this, especially when you swing out your leg or get up from a chair.
People who have osteoarthritis are more likely to experience crepitus (including 81% of people with knee arthritis), but the grinding or popping joints does not mean that you already have—or will someday definitely have—arthritis. “A grinding or or gravelly feeling, especially behind the kneecap, can be linked to changes in the cartilage,” Dr. Mehta says. “But it doesn’t always mean something is damaged.”
A previous injury to a joint makes it more likely that you’ll have crepitus in that spot. “You’re more likely to notice it in a joint you’ve injured before, such as a knee with a meniscus tear or a shoulder that has dislocated,” Dr. Mehta says.
Basically, yes, says Dr. Mehta. When we crack our knuckles, that satisfying pop we hear and feel is from the release of gas bubbles in the synovial fluid as the joint is stretched. “You’ll notice you can’t crack the same knuckle again right away,” she explains. “The gas needs time to dissolve back into the fluid.”
But the big difference between crepitus and knuckle-cracking is that crepitus is involuntary. Knuckle-cracking is a deliberate action we choose to take.
Luckily, those pops and cracks aren’t necessarily bad for your joints, even though they might sound like grinding gears on a manual transmission. Instead of worrying too much about how the joint sounds, pay attention to how the joints feel.
“If it doesn’t hurt, it’s usually nothing to worry about,” Dr. Mehta says. “The noise itself isn’t an issue. But if you feel pain, swelling or stiffness, especially if it’s getting worse over time, see an orthopedic doctor. I’d also want to see you if the joint locks, catches or gives way, or if this is a new thing that came on suddenly or after injury.”
It rarely requires emergency attention, but Dr. Mehta says to get care promptly if a joint becomes very swollen or if you can’t put weight on it after an injury. A hot, swollen joint with a fever, however, needs urgent care.
You might not be able to rid yourself of crepitus altogether, but it is possible to improve it. As long as those snaps, crackles and pops aren’t associated with any other symptoms, focusing on movement and strengthening your joints and muscles should help.
“Patients who build up their thigh and hip strength often find their knees feel better, even if the noise doesn’t fully go away,” Dr. Mehta says. “Strong muscles take pressure off the joint.”
You can do this with physical therapy, a strength-training routine in the gym, or bodyweight exercises (like squats and lunges) mixed with moderate cardio. Being at a healthy weight also takes the load off your knees and hips.

People who have osteoarthritis are more likely to experience crepitus (including 81% of people with knee arthritis), but the grinding or popping joints does not mean that you already have—or will someday definitely have—arthritis. “A grinding or or gravelly feeling, especially behind the kneecap, can be linked to changes in the cartilage,” Dr. Mehta says. “But it doesn’t always mean something is damaged.” 

Injury

A previous injury to a joint makes it more likely that you’ll have crepitus in that spot. “You’re more likely to notice it in a joint you’ve injured before, such as a knee with a meniscus tear or a shoulder that has dislocated,” Dr. Mehta says.

Is this the same thing as cracking your knuckles?

Basically, yes, says Dr. Mehta. When we crack our knuckles, that satisfying pop we hear and feel is from the release of gas bubbles in the synovial fluid as the joint is stretched. “You’ll notice you can’t crack the same knuckle again right away,” she explains. “The gas needs time to dissolve back into the fluid.”

But the big difference between crepitus and knuckle-cracking is that crepitus is involuntary. Knuckle-cracking is a deliberate action we choose to take.

Is this bad for your joints?

Luckily, those pops and cracks aren’t necessarily bad for your joints, even though they might sound like grinding gears on a manual transmission. Instead of worrying too much about how the joint sounds, pay attention to how the joints feel.

“If it doesn’t hurt, it’s usually nothing to worry about,” Dr. Mehta says. “The noise itself isn’t an issue. But if you feel pain, swelling or stiffness, especially if it’s getting worse over time, see an orthopedic doctor. I’d also want to see you if the joint locks, catches or gives way, or if this is a new thing that came on suddenly or after injury.”

It rarely requires emergency attention, but Dr. Mehta says to get care promptly if a joint becomes very swollen or if you can’t put weight on it after an injury. A hot, swollen joint with a fever, however, needs urgent care.

Is there any way to get prevent this?

You might not be able to rid yourself of crepitus altogether, but it is possible to improve it. As long as those snaps, crackles and pops aren’t associated with any other symptoms, focusing on movement and strengthening your joints and muscles should help. 

“Patients who build up their thigh and hip strength often find their knees feel better, even if the noise doesn’t fully go away,” Dr. Mehta says. “Strong muscles take pressure off the joint.”

You can do this with physical therapy, a strength-training routine in the gym, or bodyweight exercises (like squats and lunges) mixed with moderate cardio. Being at a healthy weight also takes the load off your knees and hips.

articles.title: EXCLUSIVE! Superman’s Rachel Brosnahan Reveals Her Family’s Hilarious Thanksgiving Tradition—And What She Hopes Is Next for Lois Lane
articles.content: Rachel Brosnahan knows a thing or two about playing strong, outspoken women. After winning an Emmy and two Golden Globes for her role as the quick-witted Midge Maisel in The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel, the actress traded stand-up comedy for superhero action, taking on the iconic role of Lois Lane in 2025’s Superman. And while she can certainly hold her own alongside the Man of Steel, Brosnahan has plenty of other things keeping her busy off-screen, especially with the holiday season right around the corner. In an exclusive interview with Reader’s Digest, Brosnahan gave us a peek into how she gets ready for the holidays, as well as the family traditions she looks forward to every year. She also revealed which of her famous on-screen characters she thinks would cause the most chaos at a holiday dinner party. (Spoiler alert: Midge Maisel would definitely keep things interesting.) But don’t worry, Superman fans: We didn’t forget about Lois Lane! Brosnahan also shared what it’s really like working with David Corenswet and what she hopes is next for her character in Man of Tomorrow, which hits theaters on July 9. And trust us—you’ll definitely want to hear what she has to say. Read to find out that and more. Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more celebrity interviews, fun facts, humor, cleaning, travel and tech all week long. This interview took place on Oct. 27, 2026, and has been edited for length and clarity. Reader’s Digest: You’ve played so many memorable characters, from Midge Maisel to Lois Lane. If you could invite three characters you’ve portrayed to a holiday dinner, who would make the guest list, and who would bring the most drama? Rachel Brosnahan: Midge Maisel would bring the most drama for sure. She could come. She’d keep us all entertained. I would also invite Lois Lane. I feel like she would be very practical, and she’d make sure that we had everything we needed. I play a character named Eve in a film that will likely come out sometime next year called Saturn Return. I would invite her because she’s a deeply soulful person who I feel would bring some kind of conversation starter game and really bring the heart to the gathering. Reader’s Digest: You’ve partnered with Ferrero Rocher to celebrate the holidays and the brand’s new limited-edition cinnamon spice chocolate squares. What drew you to the collaboration, and how does its message connect with the way that you personally celebrate this festive season? Rachel Brosnahan: The holidays are made by the people that you spend it with. For me, I love the holidays. It’s my favorite time of year, and it’s such a wonderful opportunity to slow down and just spend quality time with friends and family, with your neighbors. And I feel like it’s the only time we ever get to all slow down together at the same time, and so I’m so grateful for that part of it. I’ve also been such a fan of Rocher for a long time. My dad used to bring back the trays of pralines from business trips, and they made me feel very fancy. It was a year-round thing in our household, not just for the holidays. But I have such fond memories of that particular flavor, and it’s been really fun to get to try some new ones that I hadn’t tried yet, like the new cinnamon flavors. I love dark chocolate, and it just feels like the holidays in a square. Reader’s Digest: I love how you talked about bringing the family together. Is there an unforgettable or hilarious moment from a holiday gathering that your family still talks about today? Rachel Brosnahan: I’ve been celebrating the holidays with my same group of extended family since I was a little kid, and it’s been such a beloved tradition. Thanksgiving is our holiday, so we’ve all grown up together and gone from being children to adults. Now we’re at a stage where everybody is of drinking age in the family, so we have started a beloved holiday tradition to find the drunkest cousin every Thanksgiving. Whoever ends up the drunkest cousin has to get up at the end of dinner and give a very heartfelt speech. Reader’s Digest: We’re so excited to see you return as Lois Lane in Man of Tomorrow. What is one thing about playing her that surprises you, and is there a side of Lois that you’re hoping to explore next? Rachel Brosnahan: I constantly get surprised when I get introduced, mostly by the fans, to different comics that I hadn’t seen before. I’m kind of a research nerd, and I did a a pretty extensive deep dive ahead of shooting the first film. But every so often, I’ll get tagged in something or DM’d a comic that I hadn’t seen before, and it’s just so fun to see different artists’ interpretations of the character and different adventures that she goes on. James Gunn, our wonderful writer and director, knows this, but I’m dying for Lois to fight some bad guys and do a little more flying—maybe in the next one. Reader’s Digest: What is it like working with your co-star David Corenswet, aka Superman? Rachel Brosnahan: He is one of the most incisive and smart actors I’ve ever had the privilege of working with. He really sees both the whole picture and also the tiniest detail at the same time, and he’s such a wonderful collaborator. This probably wouldn’t surprise people, but he’s an accent connoisseur. You can hear many different accents in a day coming from David. Reader’s Digest: For some people, The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel and Superman are comfort watches. Do you have a favorite comfort watch during Thanksgiving or Christmas? Rachel Brosnahan: I love the film Love Actually. We watch it every year. I also love Miracle on 42nd Street. The Holiday is another one! I love all the old holiday movies. We don’t have a physical TV in our apartment, so I miss being able to turn it on and let whatever movie is on play back-to-back for a week straight. It’s one of my favorite parts of the holidays that we’ve lost a bit in the digital age, but maybe we can recreate it in some way this year. Reader’s Digest: What’s an unpopular holiday opinion that you’re willing to defend, even if it might cause an argument at the dinner table? Rachel Brosnahan: I think my unpopular holiday opinion is that you can cancel your attendance to a holiday party last minute. It’s a crazy time for people. People are navigating so many different things, and I feel like people get very sensitive about last-minute cancellations to holiday parties. Reader’s Digest: If your family and your closest friends were asked to reveal one thing about you that would completely surprise your fans, what do you think they would say? Rachel Brosnahan: This is not new information, but it’s the first thing that comes to mind because I feel like people keep getting surprised by it. Before I ran around in skirts for a living, I was an athlete, and I was on my high school wrestling team. That remains a fairly surprising fact. Reader’s Digest: As you head into the new year, what are you most looking forward to? Rachel Brosnahan: I’m sitting on so many secret updates that I can’t yet share, but I have a number of different projects that will become clearer toward the end of this year and into early next year. I’m also looking forward to the holidays this year as an opportunity to slow down, catch my breath and reconnect with people. Reader’s Digest: Dogs or cats? Rachel Brosnahan: Dogs. Reader’s Digest: Mornings or nights? Rachel Brosnahan: Nights. Reader’s Digest: What’s your favorite book? Rachel Brosnahan: Right now, it’s Joan Didion’s The Year of Magical Thinking. Reader’s Digest: What advice would you give to your younger self? Rachel Brosnahan: Invest in Microsoft. Reader’s Digest: Would you rather travel to the past or the future? Rachel Brosnahan: The past. Reader’s Digest: If you weren’t an actress, what would you be doing? Rachel Brosnahan: I think I’d be a teacher of some kind for first-graders. *Editor’s note: Reader’s Digest does not endorse any specific products or services. articles.title: Here’s Why Paper Towels Have Those Weird Patterns on Them—It’s Not Just for Looks!
articles.content:
When I steer my cart down the paper-towel aisle at the grocery store or Target, I immediately gravitate toward my favorite brand. My wife, on the other hand, seems to just grab any old thing that crosses her field of vision—which drives me crazy and is why I prefer to do the shopping whenever possible. It might sound silly, but we all have our go-tos.
In my wife’s defense, paper towels are pretty similar. Sure, some brands are stronger, thicker or use recycled paper, while others tout their innovative perforation options. But the overall concept—a quick, clean, disposable towel that’s always at the ready—spans brands and price ranges. Of course, there is one easy way to tell paper towels apart: the pattern that’s embossed on the paper.
Why do paper towels even have these patterns? They are pretty, and if you keep your paper towels on the counter, picking based on aesthetics makes sense. As long as they do the job, that is. Ahead, Jerry Ballas, who holds several patents for nonwoven paper innovations and currently serves on the board of directors for Sellars Absorbent Materials, maker of Bravo paper towels, explains what these patterns do and how they evolved.
Read on to learn all the insider info—including whether a specific type of pattern just might be superior to the rest.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more fun facts, cleaning, entertainment, tech and travel all week long.
The first paper towels hit the market more than a century ago. Here’s the story: Back in 1879 Philadelphia, two brothers named Scott started a paper-goods company, soon developing toilet paper on a roll, a major innovation at the time. “They expanded to paper towels around 1910, when they began selling Sani Towels and, eventually, Scott Towels,” Ballas says. (Yep, the same Scott Towels you can still buy today!)
“They advertised the benefits of paper towels for hygiene, convenience, utility—strong when wet, good at wiping and picking up spills—and the fact that they were disposable,” Ballas says. Advertising ultimately became a key strategy for the Scott Paper Company, according to the City University of New York, and it was one of the first American companies to lean hard into marketing and branding.
No, but it didn’t take long for the idea to catch on. “Paper towels began to be embossed in the early 1920s as a quality improvement innovation,” Ballas says. “Embossing increased liquid holding capacity and made the product thicker and softer.”
Unfortunately, embossing also made the towel somewhat weaker, so manufacturers tried to optimize the benefits while minimizing strength loss. “This was at a time when paper towels were a single-ply paper web,” Ballas says. “The embossing pattern was a very tight pattern and not highly aesthetic.”
But as the industry evolved, so did the embossing. “Around the early 1950s, a two-ply paper towel was developed that required embossing and laminating to create a pattern on the paper towel and hold the 2-plies together,” Ballas says.
It’s not just for looks … but that is a factor. At its heart, though, embossing is all about function, from how much liquid that unassuming paper towel will hold to how strong it is. Here’s the lowdown, along with some interesting facts about this household staple.
Embossing a pattern on paper towels creates pockets between the two plies of paper, which significantly increases their water-holding capacity, Ballas says. This is done through a high-pressure forming process that raises a pattern above the surface of the paper, giving it a three-dimensional effect and allowing it to absorb more liquid.
Raising a pattern on the surface makes the paper towel thicker, which contributes to a softer, squishier feel. But this also adds bulk, which despite sounding great for a towel designed to pick up spills, can cause performance to suffer. That’s because embossing can diminish the wet strength of a paper towel, which is not ideal for a product designed to be used when wet.
Ballas actually helped develop a technology called double re-creping (DRC) to tackle just this issue. The DRC technique creates a textured surface on single-ply towels, improving wet strength and reducing bulk while maintaining a softer, cloth-like feel.
Not many people want to use a kitchen paper towel that looks like it would also be at home in a gas station bathroom. So, yes, there’s also an aesthetic reason for embossing patterns on paper towels, notes Ballas. Specific patterns also make brands stand out: In a 2012 patent application for a specific embossing technique, Proctor & Gamble cited paper-product patterns as one way for manufacturers to distinguish themselves.
Embossing under high pressure also keeps the two plies of a two-ply paper towel together. That said, embossing isn’t the only way to do this; plies can also be joined through lamination, which is more like gluing, or the two processes can be combined.
Besides wanting to stand out from other paper products, manufacturers spend a lot of time and resources figuring out which patterns work best for their particular needs.
“Designs are developed and evaluated in laboratory form to define the overall results,” Ballas says. “In the end, the paper manufacturer makes the decision on the pattern chosen based on the overall benefits the pattern will deliver.”
The manufacturing techniques and scientific findings regarding TP’s patterns are pretty similar to those of paper towels. There’s one big difference, though: wet strength. Toilet paper is designed to break up quickly after use so it doesn’t clog your toilet or stick around in city wastewater-treatment facilities or your septic system.
It’s hard to definitively say which pattern is best. One study in Polymers found that micropatterns (smaller, denser patterns like dots) created more bulk and that more pronounced embossing reduced wet strength slightly. But researchers say the strength reduction was within the standard deviation. Translation: It was minimal.
Ballas says a quality paper towel comes down to a few things: strength when wet, liquid capacity and a low-lint, towel-like softness that wipes dry. But it’s hard to tell these things without trying them out.
So in the end, it mostly boils down to personal preference and experience. When I steer my cart toward my favorite paper towels, it’s because I like them enough to buy them again and again. They pick up spills, they don’t disintegrate in my hands and they don’t cost an arm and a leg. In other words, I have brand loyalty, which is something companies spend a lot of money cultivating.

Embossing under high pressure also keeps the two plies of a two-ply paper towel together. That said, embossing isn’t the only way to do this; plies can also be joined through lamination, which is more like gluing, or the two processes can be combined.

Why are all the designs different?

Besides wanting to stand out from other paper products, manufacturers spend a lot of time and resources figuring out which patterns work best for their particular needs.

“Designs are developed and evaluated in laboratory form to define the overall results,” Ballas says. “In the end, the paper manufacturer makes the decision on the pattern chosen based on the overall benefits the pattern will deliver.”

What about toilet paper patterns?

The manufacturing techniques and scientific findings regarding TP’s patterns are pretty similar to those of paper towels. There’s one big difference, though: wet strength. Toilet paper is designed to break up quickly after use so it doesn’t clog your toilet or stick around in city wastewater-treatment facilities or your septic system.

Which pattern is the most effective?

It’s hard to definitively say which pattern is best. One study in Polymers found that micropatterns (smaller, denser patterns like dots) created more bulk and that more pronounced embossing reduced wet strength slightly. But researchers say the strength reduction was within the standard deviation. Translation: It was minimal.

Ballas says a quality paper towel comes down to a few things: strength when wet, liquid capacity and a low-lint, towel-like softness that wipes dry. But it’s hard to tell these things without trying them out.

So in the end, it mostly boils down to personal preference and experience. When I steer my cart toward my favorite paper towels, it’s because I like them enough to buy them again and again. They pick up spills, they don’t disintegrate in my hands and they don’t cost an arm and a leg. In other words, I have brand loyalty, which is something companies spend a lot of money cultivating.
